newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agency's textile import quotas criticized.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agency's textile import quotas criticized.

text.p: Key members of Congress Wednesday criticized the actions of a Commerce Department body for its policies in imposing quotas on textile and apparel imports.
Commenting on a report by the General Accounting Office, they called for reforms of the procedures of the inter-agency Committee for the Implementation of Textile Agreements (CITA).
The GAO found that in 34 percent of CITA's 1990-95 decisions to impose quotas, either U.S. production had not declined or imports had not risen in the most recent year before quotas were imposed.
The congressional investigative agency also said CITA had often imposed quotas when U.S. production had increased or imports had fallen or when changes had been minimal.
It said CITA did not make public records of its meetings or allow opportunity for input from all affected parties before deciding to request consultations on quotas.

The report was released by Rep Bill Archer, R-Texas, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, Rep Philip Crane, R-Illinois, chairman of the committee's trade panel, and Sen Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, chairman of the Senate Finance subcommittee on trade.

"We believe (the report) confirms our view that broad reform of the covert procedures of the CITA bureaucray is warranted," Archer said. "The GAO report describes a hidden and erratic process at CITA which results in indefensible decisions to impose import quotas."
Archer said that "while Congress is advocating free trade, CITA is advocating protectionism."
